questions.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
questions.Question: A catheterizing patient with neurogenic lower urinary tract history develops new urgency leakage despite stable catheter timing and antimuscarinic use. What is the best next step before empiric escalation?
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. New leakage in a patient with established bladder-management complexity should prompt objective reassessment when the diagnosis or mechanism is uncertain before simply escalating therapy. Option A is incorrect because chronic urethral catheter drainage adds harm and does not define the cause of worsening leakage. Option B is incorrect because intravesical chemotherapy treats selected bladder cancer settings. Option D is incorrect because urine cytology does not evaluate storage pressure, detrusor overactivity, compliance, or outlet function. Option E is incorrect because stopping catheterization may worsen retention and upper-tract risk. Teaching point: In refractory or diagnostically uncertain urgency incontinence, bladder-function testing can distinguish detrusor overactivity, compliance problems, and outlet issues. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

questions.Source/Guideline: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
questions.Question: A stable patient has recurrent cystitis symptoms and culture data showing a susceptible lower-tract organism. Which treatment principle best fits guideline-based stewardship?
questions.Option B: Use cystoscopy as the treatment for each episode
questions.Option D: Use a short-course narrow urinary agent guided by culture
questions.Option E: Ignore susceptibility results if dysuria persists
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. Symptomatic cystitis episodes should be treated with an appropriate short-course antimicrobial selected using culture, susceptibility, and patient factors when available. Option A is incorrect because prolonged fluoroquinolone suppression is excessive when narrower episode-directed therapy fits. Option B is incorrect because cystoscopy is not antimicrobial treatment. Option C is incorrect because asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated in this recurrent uncomplicated UTI framework. Option E is incorrect because persistent or recurrent symptoms should be connected back to culture data rather than ignored. Teaching point: UTI stewardship is not just drug choice; it is matching therapy duration and spectrum to documented symptomatic infection. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
questions.Question: A healthy man has newly diagnosed high-risk localized prostate cancer and asks for focal ablation instead of standard treatment. What counseling is most guideline-concordant?
questions.Option A: Focal ablation is standard definitive therapy
questions.Option B: Observation is preferred because grade is irrelevant
questions.Option C: Discuss prostatectomy or radiation plus ADT as standard options
questions.Explanation: Option C is correct. High-risk localized prostate cancer generally requires definitive local therapy discussion, including radical prostatectomy or radiation-based treatment with appropriate systemic intensification. Option A is incorrect because focal ablation is not standard definitive management for high-risk disease. Option B is incorrect because grade and risk group drive treatment intensity. Option D is incorrect because BCG is bladder-directed therapy. Option E is incorrect because antibiotics do not treat or risk-stratify prostate cancer. Teaching point: High-risk localized prostate cancer counseling should separate investigational or focal approaches from established curative-intent pathways. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: After prior prostate radiation, a man has PSA recurrence, no metastases on imaging, and mpMRI shows a suspicious intraprostatic lesion. Local salvage is being considered. What is required next?
questions.Option E: Stop evaluation because imaging is negative
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. Before local salvage therapy after radiation, suspected local recurrence should be confirmed histologically so morbidity is not accepted for unproven disease. Option B is incorrect because cystectomy is unrelated to prostate-bed or intraprostatic salvage selection. Option C is incorrect because the suspicious lesion can guide targeted confirmation. Option D is incorrect because intravesical gemcitabine treats selected bladder cancer settings. Option E is incorrect because absence of metastases is exactly the scenario where local salvage may be considered after confirming local disease. Teaching point: Post-radiation PSA recurrence requires proof of local viable cancer before committing to salvage local therapy. Source: American Urological Association. Salvage Therapy for Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A complete TURBT shows a solitary high-grade Ta bladder tumor with muscle present and no perforation. Which management step should be considered because this is high-risk NMIBC?
questions.Option B: Induction BCG rather than surveillance alone
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. High-grade Ta NMIBC is not managed as low-risk disease; induction BCG is a guideline-supported intravesical treatment when feasible after complete resection. Option A is incorrect because office fulguration is reserved for carefully selected small low-grade recurrences, not high-grade Ta disease. Option C is incorrect because surveillance alone undertreats high-risk biology. Option D is incorrect because nephrectomy does not treat bladder-confined urothelial carcinoma. Option E is incorrect because antibiotics are not cancer therapy. Teaching point: Noninvasive stage does not equal low risk; grade and risk category drive intravesical treatment. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
questions.Question: A man has persistent CIS after adequate BCG and is fit for surgery but refuses cystectomy. Which counseling about bladder-sparing therapy is most accurate?
questions.Option C: Observation until muscle invasion is preferred
questions.Option D: Pelvic radiation is routine first salvage
questions.Option E: Cystectomy discussion remains necessary before alternatives
questions.Explanation: Option E is correct. BCG-unresponsive high-risk NMIBC should trigger a cystectomy discussion, while bladder-sparing alternatives are considered when cystectomy is refused or unsuitable. Option A is incorrect because persistent CIS after adequate BCG is not solved by indefinite BCG alone. Option B is incorrect because cytology is diagnostic surveillance, not treatment. Option C is incorrect because waiting for muscle invasion risks losing a curative window. Option D is incorrect because routine pelvic radiation is not the standard NMIBC salvage pathway. Teaching point: The board-relevant branch is not whether alternatives exist, but that they follow an explicit cystectomy suitability and refusal discussion. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A patient passes a first stone and brings the fragment to clinic. Before choosing targeted prevention, which baseline step best fits AUA stone guidance?
questions.Option E: Use urine cytology to classify the stone
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. When a stone is available, analysis helps classify stone type and direct prevention counseling and metabolic evaluation. Option B is incorrect because cystoscopy is not a routine baseline test for classifying kidney stone composition. Option C is incorrect because imaging review helps define stone burden and recurrence risk. Option D is incorrect because BCG treats selected bladder cancer settings. Option E is incorrect because urine cytology evaluates urothelial cells, not stone mineral composition. Teaching point: Stone prevention starts with objective phenotype definition: composition, burden, and risk factors before targeted drug therapy. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A recurrent calcium stone former starts chlorthalidone. Follow-up shows lower urinary calcium but new hypokalemia and low citrate. What adjustment best addresses prevention?
questions.Option B: Use urine cytology as metabolic follow-up
questions.Explanation: Option D is correct. Potassium citrate can address hypocitraturia and help correct thiazide-associated potassium/citrate problems when clinically appropriate. Option A is incorrect because fluid and dietary counseling remain part of stone prevention. Option B is incorrect because cytology does not monitor lithogenic urine chemistry. Option C is incorrect because intravesical chemotherapy does not prevent calcium stones. Option E is incorrect because cystectomy is unrelated to recurrent calcium stone prevention. Teaching point: Follow-up urine and blood testing after stone-prevention medication should change management when therapy creates new metabolic risk. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

questions.Question: A 58-year-old man with a 12 pack-year history has confirmed microhematuria with 18 RBC/hpf and no renal insufficiency. He is intermediate risk. What evaluation is recommended?
questions.Option A: Cystoscopy plus renal and bladder ultrasound
questions.Option B: Bone scan as the sole evaluation
questions.Option D: No evaluation because he is not high risk
questions.Explanation: Option A is correct. Intermediate-risk microhematuria is evaluated with cystoscopy and renal/bladder ultrasound rather than the high-risk axial imaging pathway. Option B is incorrect because bone scan does not evaluate hematuria sources. Option C is incorrect because BCG is treatment for selected bladder cancer, not diagnostic evaluation. Option D is incorrect because intermediate-risk patients still require risk-based evaluation. Option E is incorrect because prostate-bed radiation is unrelated to microhematuria workup. Teaching point: Microhematuria risk category determines the intensity of upper-tract imaging, not whether evaluation happens at all. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

questions.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline
questions.Question: A man with chronic pelvic pain has repeated negative urine cultures and STI testing. Symptoms briefly improved during prior antibiotics. What should be avoided?
questions.Option B: Repeated antibiotic courses without evidence of infection
questions.Explanation: Option B is correct. Repeated empiric antibiotics should be avoided when cultures and STI testing do not support infection, even if symptoms fluctuated during prior treatment. Option A is incorrect because phenotype-directed multimodal management is appropriate for chronic pelvic pain. Option C is incorrect because pelvic floor assessment can identify a treatable pain phenotype. Option D is incorrect because shared decision-making is central when balancing benefits and harms. Option E is incorrect because changing symptoms should prompt reassessment rather than reflex antibiotics. Teaching point: Chronic pelvic pain management should not equate transient symptom variation with occult infection. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline.
